head:
Action plans · Adult aged 30 to 45

The adult aged 30 to 45 in the thick of working life: an action plan when time and energy are short

You sit at work, you have children, you sleep less than you would like and you don't feel you have an hour to yourself. This article does not give you a tailor-made programme: that would take a coach who knows you. It gives you the trajectory that almost everyone in your situation follows, more or less: a small regular dose, strength work, slow progression, measurements, and a system to keep going. It says what the research establishes, what is a drafting proposal, and when to seek medical advice.

The question

Typical profile, illustrative

A person aged 30 to 45. Office work, eight to nine hours a day sitting, commuting included. One or two children, one of them under six. Days cut up between work, nursery or school, shopping and meals. She sleeps little, feels tired in the early afternoon, and has had no regular practice for years. She says: “I don't have time” and “in the evening, I'm wiped out”. This character is composed for the article: she does not describe a real person or a measured average.

You hear two opposite pieces of advice for this profile: three one-hour sessions a week, otherwise it's not worth it; or results with a few minutes a day. The first discourages you before you start, the second suggests that a trick can replace everything else.

What to do is no secret, and it changes little from one person to another. Taking action is not complicated when the plan is small and clear. What is hard is repeating it for weeks in a life that overflows. Adherence therefore decides the result more than the content of the plan, and it is what this article deals with first.

The question

What is the smallest dose of activity worth doing for a very busy adult aged 30 to 45, how can it be organised over 12 weeks in sessions of 20 to 30 minutes, and how can you make it last?

What is at stake

If you think you need an hour, you will do nothing in the week when you have twenty minutes. If you think four minutes are enough, you risk giving up strength work and walking for a benefit that the data do not promise. At 30-45, what you build also helps you avoid reaching 55 with a low starting point: that is reasoning, not a study result, because most of the studies cited involve older adults. Safety remains: starting small does not generally require medical clearance, but some situations, including pregnancy and the postpartum period, call for advice. The article says which ones.
rest:
The common plan, and what changes by profile

For an adult aged 18 to 64, the WHO asks for 150 to 300 minutes a week of moderate endurance, or 75 to 150 minutes of vigorous endurance, or an equivalent combination, plus muscle strengthening at least two days a week. Activity counts whatever the length of each bout: the 10-minute minimum rule has been removed.3 This base is common. What varies by profile:

What changes, according to the WHO
  • Ages 18 to 64: the volumes above. Generally no prior medical clearance, unless there is a contraindication; see a professional if new symptoms appear when you increase.3
  • Age 65 and over: the same volumes, plus varied activity that emphasises balance and strength, at least three days a week.3
  • Pregnancy and postpartum: at least 150 minutes of moderate activity a week without contraindication, strengthening, the pelvic floor; start small if you were not active; specialist advice to go beyond the recommendations.3

For you, the starting point is low, the main obstacle is time and energy, and sitting work calls for one more gesture. We follow five steps, from the general to the specific.

Step 1 of 5 · Time

Free time is reduced, it is not nil

The American Time Use Survey, an official US survey, publishes average hours per day by presence of children. In 2024, adults whose youngest child is under 6 report 3.20 hours of leisure and sports per day, against 4.09 hours if the youngest is 6 to 17 and 5.64 hours with no child under 18.1

With a child under six, free time is shorter and caregiving time is longer

Adult averages, American Time Use Survey 2024, United States. “Leisure and sports” includes television. Source: Bureau of Labor Statistics.1

What this means

With a child under six, there are about 2 h 26 less leisure time per day (5.64 minus 3.20, derived calculation), and caregiving time goes from 0.08 to 2.57 hours. The lack of time is real. But 150 minutes a week is about 21 minutes a day (derived), a little over a tenth of those 3.20 hours. The question becomes: where do you put 20 minutes that will last?

Caveats: these figures are American, averages, all days combined; “leisure and sports” includes television; and the “personal care” item, which includes sleep, is 9.50 hours with a child under six against 9.86 without a child, that is 22 minutes less (derived), which says nothing about sleep alone. The Insee Time Use survey (2010) gives 5 h 11 of free time per day for adults in urban France, with no breakdown for parents of young children in the extract read.2

Step 2 of 5 · The smallest useful dose

Very small doses produce effects, but not the same ones

Two questions get mixed up. Are brief efforts slipped into the day linked to better health? Do short planned sessions improve fitness?

Brief efforts during the day

The UK Biobank followed 25,241 people who did no exercise (mean age 61.8) with a wrist sensor, for 6.9 years on average, with 852 deaths. The sensor picked up intense bursts of everyday life, which the team calls VILPA: running for a bus, walking very fast with your shopping, playing energetically with children.4,5

In adults who do not exercise, a few brief efforts go with a lower risk of death

25,241 adults with no reported exercise, mean age 61.8, 852 deaths. Association observed. Source: Stamatakis et al., Nature Medicine, 2022 (abstract).4,5

What this means

Three efforts of one to two minutes a day go with a risk of death 38 to 40% lower all-cause, and 48 to 49% lower for cardiovascular causes. A tiny dose is therefore not useless. But the mean age is 61.8: at 30-45, you cannot transpose it. The study is observational, and the record read is an abstract without a confidence interval.4,5 Keep the direction, not the percentage. For the minimum dose, see the article “The minimum effective dose: how much, what, how often” in the series.

Short planned sessions

In a trial by Gillen and colleagues, sedentary men of about 27 did 12 weeks of training, three times a week. One group did 10-minute sessions: three all-out 20-second sprints, 2 minutes of easy pedalling between each, warm-up and cool-down included. The other did 50 minutes of continuous moderate cycling.6

Ten minutes of sprints, three times a week, improved fitness as much as 50 minutes of cycling

Sedentary men of about 27, 25 analysed including 6 controls. The 30 minutes include warm-up and cool-down. Source: Gillen et al., PLoS ONE, 2016.6

What this means

With five times less time (30 minutes against 150 a week, derived), the sprint group gained as much VO2peak (19%) and improved insulin sensitivity more (53% against 34%), with no significant difference between the groups. But the trial has 25 participants analysed including 6 controls, all sedentary men, and its authors note that all-out sprints demand a lot of motivation. The plan below uses sustained intervals, not all-out ones.6

A meta-analysis of 53 randomised trials in 1,514 adults aged 19 to 47, so your age range, compares interval protocols. In healthy adults, low-volume sessions (5 minutes or less according to the authors) improve VO2max by 3.96 mL/kg/min compared with no training (interval 2.73 to 5.18, six trials), with no difference from continuous moderate exercise (0.20, from -1.53 to 1.94). Intervals of 2 minutes or more give 7.62 (5.36 to 9.88). The authors conclude that intervals of 2 minutes or more and sessions of 15 minutes or more are needed to maximise the effect, and point to strong heterogeneity and possible publication bias.7 This concerns exercise capacity, not lifespan, and does not say that intervals replace strength work or walking.

Step 3 of 5 · The sitting day

Breaking up sitting changes the body's response, at least in the short term

A meta-analysis of 34 studies and 1,331,468 participants associates each additional hour of sitting with 1% more risk of death up to 8 hours a day, and with 4% beyond.9 This is an observational link. For a more direct measure, Dunstan and colleagues had 19 overweight or obese adults aged 45 to 65 go through three five-hour sessions in the laboratory after a meal rich in sugar and fat: sitting without interruption, with 2 minutes of slow walking every 20 minutes, or with 2 minutes of faster walking.8

Interrupting sitting reduces the rise in blood glucose after a meal

19 overweight adults aged 45 to 65, crossover trial. Bars 75.9 and 70.4: derived (100 minus 24.1 and 29.6). Source: Dunstan et al., Diabetes Care, 2012.8

What this means

The breaks reduced the rise in blood glucose by 24.1% and 29.6%, and the insulin response by about 23%. Even a slow break changes how your body handles a meal. This is an effect lasting a few hours, in the laboratory, in older adults: not evidence on lifespan, and the trial's rhythm has not been validated in real life.8

The WHO writes that replacing sedentary time with activity of any intensity, even light, brings benefits.3 Furniture does not solve everything: according to a Cochrane review (34 studies), sit-stand desks reduce sitting time by 84 to 116 minutes per working day, with very low-quality evidence and health effects not demonstrated.10 For details, see article No. 07 in the series.

Step 4 of 5 · Strength

Two strength sessions a week are recommended, and they can be short

The WHO recommends muscle strengthening that works all the major muscle groups, at least two days a week: a strong recommendation, moderate-certainty evidence.3 A meta-analysis of 16 cohorts associates strength training alone with a risk ratio for death of 0.85 (0.79 to 0.93) and its combination with endurance, compared with neither, with 0.60 (0.54 to 0.67). The dose associated with the lowest risk is about 40 minutes a week, with certainty of evidence judged very low.11

What this means

Two sessions of 20 to 30 minutes make 40 to 60 minutes a week (derived), the same order of magnitude, without proving anything: the 40 minutes is a group benchmark. What to take away is that strength work does not require long sessions and that, combined with endurance, it goes with a lower risk. No source read gives the ideal frequency for this profile: the “twice” comes from the WHO.

Step 5 of 5 · Pregnancy and postpartum

Moving is generally encouraged, but this case calls for a professional

The WHO recommends that pregnant and postpartum women without contraindication do at least 150 minutes of moderate aerobic activity a week, with strengthening and pelvic floor exercises, which can be done every day to reduce the risk of urinary incontinence. Those who were not active start small and increase gradually; those who did vigorous exercise before pregnancy can continue it; those aiming for competition or clearly exceeding the recommendations should be followed by a specialist, and anyone with warning signs should seek care immediately.3

ACOG Committee Opinion No. 804 points the same way: encourage starting or continuing exercise, which is safe and desirable in the absence of complications and contraindications, with modifications sometimes needed. Observational studies associate it with less gestational diabetes and fewer caesarean deliveries and with a shorter recovery.12 I read only its summary. A secondary summary repeats its stop signs (bleeding, abdominal pain, regular contractions, fluid leakage, breathlessness before exertion, dizziness, headache, chest pain, weakness that affects balance, calf pain or swelling).13

What this means

The message is favourable, not restrictive. But the detail (when to resume after childbirth, what to avoid, what to do for the pelvic floor, what to adapt after a complicated pregnancy) depends on your situation. I could not read an official timeframe for resuming and I do not give one. Talk to your doctor, your midwife or a professional trained in pelvic floor rehabilitation (drafting suggestion), and follow the plan below only with their agreement.

Real obstacles, and how to remove them

Habit takes longer than people say

In the study by Lally and colleagues, 96 university volunteers (mean age 27) repeated an action every day in the same context and recorded for 84 days how automatic it was becoming. The plateau is reached in about 66 days, from 18 to 254 depending on the person; exercise took longer (91 days in this subgroup, difference not significant). An isolated miss did not disturb progress; many misses lowered the final level.16,17

The time it takes for an action to become automatic varies greatly from one person to another

The top of the range is extrapolated beyond the 84 days of observation. 96 volunteers, according to two accounts (original article not read). Source: Lally et al., 2010.16,17

What this means

A 12-week plan lasts 84 days: it is not the finish line. At 12 weeks, it may not yet be automatic, and that is normal. Miss a session, pick up again at the next one. Limits: only 39 of the 82 participants gave usable curves, the measure is self-reported, and the accounts read report the 66 days sometimes as a mean, sometimes as a median.16,17 The advice that follows: one simple action, repeated at the same time and in the same place.17

From intention to action: say when, where, how

An “implementation intention” is a plan of the type “when this situation arises, I do this action”: “after dropping the children off, I walk for 20 minutes”. A meta-analysis of 94 studies (Gollwitzer and Sheeran, 2006, according to an account) finds a mean effect of d = 0.65 on goal attainment; an update covering 642 tests gives 0.27 to 0.66 depending on format, motivation and repetition.18 In a randomised trial on exercise (248 participants), increasing motivation alone raised intentions but not sessions significantly; adding an implementation intention had “a dramatic effect” on later exercise (abstract read, without percentages).19 Motivation is not enough, and above all it is not a system: writing down the time and place in advance turns “I should” into an appointment. The effect is medium to large, never guaranteed.

Measuring to keep going

A meta-regression of 122 evaluations (44,747 adults) finds an overall effect of 0.31 on activity and diet. Self-monitoring is the technique that explains the most of the differences between studies (13% out of 26); combined with another control technique, it goes with an effect of 0.42 against 0.26 for other interventions. Heterogeneity is strong (69%) and this is an association between studies.20 In practice: tick off each session done and redo the THW tests.

Energy and sleep

A consensus of the American Academy of Sleep Medicine and the Sleep Research Society (15 experts, 5,314 articles) recommends that adults get at least 7 hours of sleep a night, on a regular basis. Sleeping less is associated with weight gain, diabetes, hypertension, heart disease, depression, more pain and more accidents; the text specifies that needs vary and that these are associations.14 A meta-analysis of 66 studies finds that regular exercise has small beneficial effects on sleep duration and efficiency and medium effects on its quality (abstract, no figures).15

What this means

Do not take your slot from your sleep: if the only free moment makes you sleep less than 7 hours, 20 minutes at midday are better than 20 minutes at 5:30 a.m. (drafting reasoning). Regular exercise does not harm sleep in this synthesis, it improves it a little. I have not read a solid source on the effect of activity on stress or fatigue: I do not assert it.

The three-phase action plan

This plan is a drafting proposal built from the sources above, not a protocol tested as such: the mean gains cited come from trials, the exact shape of the weeks is a choice. It is aimed at an adult without contraindication and not pregnant (step 5), with sessions of 20 to 30 minutes at a fixed time.

Common rules. A slot set in advance in the diary, with the when and the where. An effort of 5 to 6 out of 10 for moderate (you speak in full sentences but you would not sing), 7 to 8 out of 10 for vigorous (a few words at a time), scales taken from the WHO.3 Between sessions, two gestures with no slot: an active break of 2 to 3 minutes per hour sitting, and two or three brief efforts a day (stairs at a brisk pace, speeding up for a bus). These are drafting choices inspired by Dunstan and the VILPA study, not validated protocols.

The dose rises in four-week steps, with a lighter week for each retest

Drafting proposal, untested: sums of the sessions in each phase. THW tests at weeks 1, 6 and 12. Walking, commuting and active breaks are not counted.

Phase 1, weeks 1 to 4: settle in Proposal

60 to 75 minutes of sessions per week, 3 slots of 20 to 25 minutes.

  • Two moderate endurance slots: brisk walking, cycling or rowing, 20 minutes (25 from week 3), effort 5 to 6 out of 10.
  • One strength slot at home, 20 minutes (25 from week 3): squat, lunge, incline push-ups, band row, glute bridge, plank. Two sets of 8 to 12 repetitions, effort 6 to 7 out of 10 at the end of the set.
  • Week 1: baseline test.

To move on: at least 9 sessions out of 12 done (75%, drafting threshold). If not, repeat phase 1 without guilt: an isolated miss counts for little.16

Phase 2, weeks 5 to 8: build up Proposal

95 minutes of sessions per week, 4 slots of 20 to 25 minutes; week 6 lightened to 70 minutes for the retest.

  • Two full-body strength slots of 25 minutes: add repetitions, then load.
  • One moderate endurance slot of 25 minutes.
  • One interval slot of 20 minutes: 5 minutes of warm-up, then 6 times 1 minute at 7 to 8 out of 10 with 1 minute 30 of easy recovery; weeks 7 and 8: 4 times 2 minutes with 2 minutes of recovery, because intervals of 2 minutes or more give the greatest gain.7

To move on: at least 12 sessions out of 16. To step back: fewer than 9 sessions out of 16, or tiredness at the end of the week several weeks in a row: go back to the phase 1 dose for two weeks.

Phase 3, weeks 9 to 12: consolidate Proposal

105 to 115 minutes of sessions per week, 4 slots of 25 to 30 minutes; week 12 lightened to 80 minutes for the retest.

  • Two strength slots of 30 minutes.
  • One moderate endurance slot of 30 minutes.
  • One interval slot of 25 minutes: 5 minutes of warm-up, 5 times 2 minutes at 7 to 8 out of 10, 2 minutes of recovery.

Afterwards, maintenance: keep the four slots. The plan provides 40 to 55 minutes of endurance a week in sessions: on its own it does not reach the bottom of the WHO window. The rest, if you manage it, comes from walking and the day's efforts, since any duration counts.3

A typical week, to adapt

  • Monday: 20 minutes of brisk walking at the lunch break.
  • Wednesday: 20 minutes of strength at home, just before the evening meal.
  • Saturday: 25 minutes of endurance, with the family if possible.
  • Every day: an active break for every hour sitting.

The principle: link each session to a moment you already meet every day, not to a time of good intentions. This is the implementation intention applied to the diary.18

The retests: three measurements, no more

Do the THW tests at weeks 1, 6 and 12, under the same conditions (surface, time of day, warm-up). For this profile, endurance and strength are the useful tests; mobility is a good complement after years of sitting in a chair. The THW protocols and norm tables were not provided to me: the article promises no score.

  • The score improves beyond the noise of the test (in the Cooper test, the variation from one attempt to the next is about 52 metres in 15 recreational runners21): keep going.
  • It stagnates at week 6: do not conclude anything from a single test. Check the sessions done, your sleep and the real intensity of the intervals, then continue to week 12.
  • It drops clearly: rest for a week and redo the test; if the drop persists with unusual tiredness, talk to a health professional.

Common mistakes, warning signs, when to see a professional

  • Starting too big.The WHO says to start with small amounts and increase gradually.3
  • Stopping everything after a missed week.Sick child, trip: resume at the dose of the current phase or the previous one.16
  • Replacing everything with a few minutes of brief efforts.The data read are associations in older adults, not proof that they replace walking and strength work.4
  • Cutting into your sleep, changing programme every two weeks, testing too often.Below a regular 7 hours, the unfavourable associations add up;14 repetition in the same context builds automaticity;17 between two closely spaced tests, the difference is noise.21
Warning signs: stop and seek medical advice
  • Pain or tightness in the chest, breathlessness abnormal for the effort, feeling faint, dizziness or palpitations (drafting list, not taken from a document read). The WHO says to see a professional if new symptoms appear when you increase activity.3
  • Known illness (heart, lungs, metabolism, joints), treatment that affects exertion, current injury: seek advice before starting.
  • Pregnancy or postpartum: advice from the professional who follows you, before and during.
  • Snoring with daytime sleepiness or unrefreshing sleep: the consensus recommends seeing a professional if a sleep disorder is suspected.14

The official screening lists (PAR-Q+, ACSM, HAS) could not be read for this version: the cases above come from the WHO and from the drafting, they do not form a complete list.

The answer to the question

What is solid. The base is common: 150 to 300 minutes moderate or 75 to 150 vigorous, plus strength work two days a week, any duration counting.3 In trials, interval sessions of 15 to 30 minutes improve fitness as much as continuous moderate exercise in adults aged 19 to 47.6,7 Breaking up sitting changes the response of sugar and insulin after a meal, in the short term.8 Adherence tools exist (same context, “when, where, how” plan, self-monitoring), with mean effects, never guaranteed.17,18,20

What is probable. A tiny dose is not useless: brief efforts and a little strength work go with a lower risk, but in people much older than you and in observation only.4,11 At 12 weeks, the concrete benefit for you is fitness and the ability to keep up a rhythm, not mortality.

What is a proposal. The three phases, the doses, the 75% thresholds, the active breaks, the retests. What remains uncertain: the effect of each element for you, the benefit at 30-45 on lifespan, the minimum dose of strength work, and everything to do with pregnancy and postpartum.

In one sentence: choose a fixed slot, a 20-minute walk and a strength session, write down when and where, repeat for 12 weeks, measure. Regularity does the work.

What these figures do not say
  • The study on brief efforts concerns adults of 61.8 on average, in observation.4
  • The Gillen trial (25 sedentary men analysed) and the Dunstan trial (19 overweight adults aged 45 to 65) are small.6,8
  • The free-time figures come from an American survey (2024) and a French survey (2010), as averages.1,2
  • No source read tests this 12-week plan.

Frequently asked questions

Do sessions have to last at least 10 minutes?

No, the WHO removed this rule. To improve fitness, the authors of the meta-analysis recommend sessions of 15 minutes or more.3,7

Are a few minutes of effort a day enough?

They go with a lower risk in adults over 60 who did not exercise, not with proof that they replace strength and endurance work.4

I am pregnant or have given birth: can I follow this plan?

Not without advice. The WHO and ACOG encourage activity in the absence of contraindications, but the detail depends on your situation: ask your doctor or midwife.3,12

I sleep six hours: should I still train?

Start small without cutting into your sleep: the consensus recommends 7 hours or more, and regular exercise improves sleep a little. If you think you have a sleep disorder, see a professional.14,15
